name: Buteyko breathing
lead: The Buteyko method is a breathing retraining system developed by Ukrainian physiologist Konstantin Buteyko in the Soviet Union in the 1950s. Its three principles are nasal breathing, reduced breathing, and relaxation, and it is based on the theory that chronic over-breathing (hyperventilation) causes or worsens conditions such as asthma.[1]

In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed as a way to encourage nasal breathing, calm anxiety and, by extension, support facial development and mouth-breathing correction, and some users pair it with mouth taping during sleep.[2] Research has focused almost entirely on asthma, with small trials showing some improvement in symptoms and quality of life but little effect on lung function.[1][3][4]

paras: Practitioners use the control pause, the time a person can comfortably hold their breath after exhaling, as a measure of progress; they say improvement appears as a longer pause and lower pulse rate.[1] Proponents claim the method can help many conditions, including asthma, COPD and chronic hyperventilation, and some advocates cite up to 150 conditions.[1]

A first official study of the method on asthma was conducted in 1968 at the Leningrad Institute of Pulmonology, and in 1980 a Soviet health ministry order (No. 591) called for implementing it for bronchial asthma. It later spread to Australia, New Zealand, Britain and the United States.[1]

A 1998 blinded randomized trial of 39 people with asthma in Australia compared Buteyko techniques with control classes and measured medication use and lung function.[5] A 2003 randomized trial of 90 people with asthma compared Buteyko breathing, a pranayama-mimicking device and a dummy device over six months, examining bronchial responsiveness and symptoms.[6] Other randomized trials have examined Buteyko as an adjunct to conventional asthma management, taught by video, and compared with pranayama for quality of life.[3][7][8]

A 2020 Cochrane review of breathing exercises for adults with asthma, covering Buteyko among other methods, found that exercises may improve quality of life and hyperventilation symptoms, with moderate to very low certainty.[4] Reviewers noted small samples, inconsistent designs and difficulty with blinding.[1] A 2014 Scottish (SIGN) guideline said the method may improve some symptoms and quality of life but has little effect on lung function, and a 2015 Australian government review found no clear evidence of effectiveness.[1] A 2008 study examined whether breath-hold time relates to end-tidal CO2 as Buteyko proposed.[10] No trials were found on the use of Buteyko breathing for facial appearance or nasal shape.

On looksmax.org, one thread titled as a Buteyko method post describes it as a free way to reduce anxiety and asthma symptoms, and argues that breathing less raises carbon dioxide and produces calm.[2] A reply links mouth breathing to palate and tonsil changes and says correct nighttime breathing is hard with such changes, and another user reports taping the mouth with micropore tape while sleeping.[2] These are user claims; no published studies tested them.

lore.intro: Buteyko breathing is discussed on looksmax.org as a breathing and calming practice linked to nasal breathing and mouth-breathing concerns.[2]

claims.claim: Breathing less raises CO2 and calms anxiety
claims.believers: A forum poster says reduced breathing helps anxiety better than benzodiazepines and compares the effect to sedatives.[2]
claims.experts: No trials of anxiety outcomes were found in the cited research; critics note a lack of research that hyperventilation and low CO2 cause disease.[1]

claims.claim: It improves asthma more than medication
claims.believers: The same poster says it helped his asthma much more than medication.[2]
claims.experts: Trials report possible symptom and quality-of-life benefits with little effect on lung function, and reviews rate certainty as low.[1][4]

claims.claim: Damage from mouth breathing makes nighttime nasal breathing hard, prompting mouth taping
claims.believers: Users say mouth breathing alters the palate and tonsils and describe taping the mouth with micropore tape during sleep.[2]
claims.experts: The sources reviewed contain no studies on this link or on mouth taping.

card.summary: A breathing-retraining method built around nasal, reduced breathing; asthma trials show modest symptom effects and none test it for looks.
card.note: Studied for asthma only; claims about appearance are untested.

quick.overview:
The Buteyko method teaches nasal, reduced breathing and relaxation, based on the theory that chronic over-breathing drives conditions such as asthma. It was developed in the Soviet Union in the 1950s.

Trials in asthma suggest possible symptom and quality-of-life benefits with little change in lung function. In looksmaxxing forums it is discussed alongside nasal breathing and mouth taping, but no studies test it for appearance.
quick.mechanism: Practitioners aim to reduce breathing volume, breathe through the nose and relax, tracking progress with a breath-hold time called the control pause.
quick.risks: The sources reviewed describe no specific adverse events. Medical commentators object to broad claims, such as reduced medication use, that lack adequate evidence.
